For it always begins there, where it ends. Through the cycle of all these things, just as the mind itself willed, it fashioned animals from the lower elements that were devoid of reason. For it did not bestow reason. The air brought forth flying creatures, while the water brought forth swimming ones. The water and the earth were also separated from one another in the manner that pleased the mind. Afterward, the earth gave birth to the living creatures it had contained within: namely, quadrupeds, creeping things, wild beasts, and domestic animals alike. But the father of all, being life and brilliance, created man similar to himself and rejoiced in him as if he were his own son. For he was beautiful, and he bore the image of his own father. Indeed, God, clearly delighted with his own true form, granted all his works for human use. But man, <margin>note the sin of the philosophers <unclear>what it may be</unclear></margin>
having observed the creation of all things in his father, wished himself to create as well. Whence he fell from the contemplation of the father to the sphere of generation. And although he possessed power over all things, he took note of the handiwork of the seven governors. These, rejoicing in the meditation of the human mind, each made him a participant in their own order.

<summary>This passage describes the creation of the natural world by the divine Mind, the subsequent creation of man in the image of God, and man's eventual descent from divine contemplation into the realm of material generation.</summary>
<keywords>Creation, Divine Mind, Human Nature, Seven Governors, Generation, Philosophy</keywords>
